decks.domain: Traffic flow, traffic stops, sharing the road, trucks and school buses

cards.front: What can greatly increase the stopping distance you need?
cards.back: Weather, road conditions, traffic volume and time of day can greatly increase the stopping distance you need.

cards.front: Why should you keep to the limits and the pace of traffic?
cards.back: Keep to posted limits and the pace of traffic; much faster means constant passing, and much slower causes back-ups and unpredictability.

cards.front: How does a zipper merge work?
cards.back: At a zipper merge where two lanes become one, use both lanes equally until just before the closure, then take turns into the open lane; drivers who wait until the lane ends are doing it right.

cards.front: Is using the closing lane right up to the merge point cutting in?
cards.back: In a zipper merge, using the closing lane up to the merge point is correct, not cutting in.

cards.front: Which places are slow zones that call for lower speed and extra attention?
cards.back: Slow zones calling for lower speed and extra attention include shopping centers, schools, parks and playgrounds, residential streets, rush hour, narrow bridges, toll plazas and rail crossings.

decks.domain: Traffic flow, traffic stops, sharing the road, trucks and school buses

cards.front: On what basis do officers make traffic stops?
cards.back: Officers make traffic stops on reasonable suspicion of a traffic or criminal violation.

cards.front: What should you do when emergency lights or a siren appear behind you?
cards.back: When you see emergency lights or hear a siren behind you, stay calm, signal and pull off or to the right as soon as it is safe; the officer may ask you to move farther from traffic.

cards.front: What should you do once you have stopped for an officer?
cards.back: Once stopped, shut off the engine and audio, stay inside unless told otherwise, use interior lights at night, keep hands visible and follow instructions.

cards.front: What should you do about windows, weapons and documents when the officer arrives?
cards.back: The officer may come to either side; lower that window, mention any weapon in the vehicle at first contact without reaching for it, and wait for instructions before reaching for documents.

cards.front: What can you do if an officer out of uniform does not show credentials?
cards.back: An officer not in uniform will normally show credentials, and you may ask to see them if they do not.

cards.front: What will the officer usually ask for, and what if it is out of reach?
cards.back: The officer will usually explain the stop and ask for your license, proof of insurance and registration; if those are out of reach, say where they are and wait for an okay before getting them.

cards.front: What should you do if asked to step out, and what outcomes are possible?
cards.back: If asked to step out, keep your hands visible and stand where directed; the officer may give a warning, a ticket that may carry a fine, or make an arrest, and you may ask what action is being taken.

cards.front: Where should you contest an officer's decision?
cards.back: Do not argue at the roadside; contest a decision in court instead, and ask for a supervisor soon after the stop if you think the officer acted improperly.

cards.front: Does signing a traffic ticket admit guilt, and what if you refuse?
cards.back: Signing a traffic ticket does not admit guilt, but refusing to sign it can lead to arrest.

cards.front: How do signing a ticket, refusing to sign and disagreeing differ?
cards.back: Signing a ticket is not admitting guilt, but refusing to sign can get you arrested; disagreements go to court, not the roadside.

decks.domain: Traffic flow, traffic stops, sharing the road, trucks and school buses

cards.front: What does sharing the road mean?
cards.back: Sharing the road means everyone has the right to use it and the duty to obey traffic laws and watch out for one another, keeping in mind that bicycles, motorcycles, buses and trucks handle differently.

cards.front: What is motorcycle lane filtering, and when is it allowed?
cards.back: Lane filtering lets a two-wheeled motorcycle pass stopped vehicles in its lane when traffic in neighboring lanes is also stopped, there is room, and it goes no faster than fifteen miles per hour.

cards.front: What are the limits on motorcycle lane filtering?
cards.back: Lane filtering is limited to two-wheeled motorcycles passing stopped traffic at no more than fifteen miles per hour, not moving traffic.

cards.front: What causes most motorist crashes with bicycles or motorcycles?
cards.back: Most motorist-caused crashes with bicycles or motorcycles involve a driver turning left in front of the oncoming rider, so look for riders at the right of the lane or on the shoulder, look again and judge their speed first.

cards.front: What rights and duties do bicycles have on the road?
cards.back: Bicycles are vehicles under state law with the same duty to obey rules, signs and markings; at normal traffic speed they may use the full lane, on a multi-lane one-way street they may ride on either side, and you should not honk to startle them.

decks.domain: Traffic flow, traffic stops, sharing the road, trucks and school buses

cards.front: What are No Zones around trucks and buses?
cards.back: No Zones are blind areas around trucks and buses where cars vanish from view or sit so close the driver cannot stop or maneuver safely, which greatly raises crash risk.

cards.front: Why should you never pass or stop close behind a backing truck?
cards.back: Never pass or stop close behind a truck or bus that is backing or about to back, because the trailer hides objects in its No Zone.

cards.front: Why should you not tailgate a truck or bus?
cards.back: Do not tailgate a truck or bus: its driver cannot see you behind it, and it blocks your own view of traffic.

cards.front: How do truck and bus side blind spots compare with a car's?
cards.back: Trucks and buses have much larger side blind spots than cars, so a sudden lane change or emergency move by the driver could hit you there.

decks.domain: Traffic flow, traffic stops, sharing the road, trucks and school buses

cards.front: Why should you stay behind white stop bars at signs and signals?
cards.back: Trucks and buses need more room to turn and change lanes, so stay behind white stop bars at signs and signals, which are often placed to leave trucks turning room.

cards.front: How should you pass a truck, and when may you cut back in front?
cards.back: Pass trucks quickly and on the left when you can, and do not cut back in front until both of its headlights show in your rearview mirror, since trucks need longer to slow down.

cards.front: What test tells you when to return in front of a truck after passing?
cards.back: Returning in front of a truck after passing uses the same test as any pass: wait until both of its headlights appear in your rearview mirror.

cards.front: Why should you never squeeze between a truck and the curb?
cards.back: Trucks and buses often swing into the left lane to turn right, so never squeeze between one and the curb or shoulder.

cards.front: What is a truck doing when it moves into the left lane before a right turn?
cards.back: A truck or bus moving into the left lane before a right turn is setting up a wide turn; do not slip between it and the curb or shoulder.

cards.front: What are runaway truck ramps for, and what may you not do on them?
cards.back: Runaway truck ramps stop vehicles whose brakes fail; chaining up, changing a tire or parking on a ramp or its entrance is illegal and unsafe.

cards.front: What is one sign of a runaway truck or bus, and what should you do?
cards.back: Smoke from the brakes is one sign of a runaway truck or bus, so get out of its way and never get in front of it.

decks.domain: Traffic flow, traffic stops, sharing the road, trucks and school buses

cards.front: Why should you stay alert behind buses?
cards.back: Buses stop often, so stay alert behind them, and take care passing a stopped bus because it may pull into your lane.

cards.front: Who has the right of way when a bus pulls out of a drop-off spot?
cards.back: A bus pulling out of a drop-off spot into traffic has the right-of-way, and you should watch for riders waiting, getting off or loading bikes in front of it.

cards.front: Where should you take extra care near school buses?
cards.back: Take extra care near school buses in neighborhoods and school zones, where students board, leave and cross the road.

cards.front: What do overhead yellow lights on a school bus mean?
cards.back: Overhead yellow warning lights mean a school bus is about to stop for children and stay on until the door opens, when the red STOP lights and STOP arm come on.

cards.front: What are the two stages of school bus lights?
cards.back: School bus lights come in two stages: yellow means the bus is about to stop, red with the STOP arm means the door is open and you must stop.

cards.front: How far from a school bus must you stop, and until when?
cards.back: Stay stopped at least twenty feet from the front or rear bumper of a school bus until the driver pulls in the STOP arm and turns off the red lights; failing to stop is illegal.

cards.front: What do you do when a school bus shows alternating flashing red lights?
cards.back: When a school bus shows alternating flashing red lights from front or rear, stop at least twenty feet before it and go on carefully only after the lights stop.

decks.module: Who stops for a school bus
decks.domain: Traffic flow, traffic stops, sharing the road, trucks and school buses

cards.front: On which roads must traffic in both directions stop for a school bus?
cards.back: On a divided highway of four or more lanes with a median, only traffic behind the school bus must stop; on a two-lane road, or a four-lane road with no median, traffic both ways must stop.

cards.front: On a highway with five or more lanes and a center turn lane, who stops for a school bus?
cards.back: Where a highway has a shared center turn lane and five or more lanes, the duty to stop falls only on the lanes behind the bus, not on oncoming traffic.

cards.front: When does oncoming traffic have to stop for a school bus?
cards.back: Whether oncoming traffic stops for a school bus depends on the road: yes on two-lane roads and four-lane roads without a median, no on divided highways with a median or roads of five or more lanes with a center turn lane.

decks.domain: Traffic flow, traffic stops, sharing the road, trucks and school buses

cards.front: Why should you never turn in front of a light rail vehicle?
cards.back: A light rail vehicle can weigh up to forty tons and cannot stop quickly, so never turn in front of one and check every direction before turning across light rail tracks.

cards.front: What should you watch for in light rail areas?
cards.back: In light rail areas watch for riders boarding and leaving, and stay alert because buildings and plants can hide the trains.

cards.front: What do lights and gates at a light rail crossing mean?
cards.back: Traffic lights, warning lights and gates at light rail crossings all mean stop and do not cross; never drive around a gate, even right after a train passes, since another may come from the other way.

cards.front: How should you treat a hanging light rail wire?
cards.back: Light rail overhead wires hang at a standard eighteen feet, six inches above the track center; treat any hanging wire as live, never touch it, and report it or faulty safety devices to RTD.

cards.front: How do you treat a railroad crossbuck, and what does the sign below it show?
cards.back: Treat a railroad crossbuck like a yield sign, and a sign below it shows how many tracks the crossing has when there is more than one.

cards.front: How does a crossbuck differ from flashing lights or gates at a rail crossing?
cards.back: A crossbuck is treated like a yield sign, while flashing lights or gates at a light rail crossing mean stop and do not cross.

cards.front: Which vehicles must stop at most railroad crossings?
cards.back: Commercial buses and hazardous-materials trucks must stop at most railroad crossings, so be ready to stop when following one.

recap_hooks.text: Conditions stretch stopping distance, keep pace with traffic, and use both lanes in a zipper merge.
At a stop, pull right, stay inside with hands visible, and wait before reaching for documents.
Signing a ticket is not admitting guilt; contest it in court.
Bicycles are vehicles, and most crashes with riders come from drivers turning left in front of them.
Stay out of truck No Zones, never tailgate, and never stop behind a backing truck.
Pass trucks quickly on the left and return only when both headlights show; never squeeze in on a wide right turn.
Yellow bus lights warn, red lights and the STOP arm mean stop at least twenty feet back.

recaps.module: Who stops for a school bus

recap_hooks.text: Oncoming traffic stops for a school bus unless a median divides the road or a center turn lane splits five or more lanes.
Never turn in front of light rail or drive around gates, and treat a crossbuck like a yield sign.
